source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC3348338. This is the author manuscript (NIHMS348105) of Addiction 2012;107(7):1246-1260, not the publisher's version. Read in full in the built-in browser: abstract, introduction, methods, results, Tables 1-5 (Table 1 designs and stratification tallied), discussion, limitations, implications, acknowledgments with funding and interests, declarations, reference list (refs 29 and 36 checked). Figures 1-3 (flow chart and dose-response curves) not examined as images; their key values are in Table 3 and the text.

claims.overstatement: Reference group and design. The statement calls this 'a review that compared only with lifetime abstainers', set inside a claim about prospective cohort studies. In fact, where a primary study's reference was current non-drinkers, mortality RRs were corrected for former drinkers with an external factor (from the authors' 2011 meta-analysis), and morbidity RRs were left uncorrected. So part of the 'lifetime abstainer' comparison is a modelled correction or a current non-drinker group. The review also pooled 12 case-control studies with 32 cohorts (6 of the 24 fully stratified studies are case-control, all for morbidity). It did not require participants to be free of heart disease at baseline (it excluded only samples made up entirely of high-risk people).
claims.note: All numbers attributed to Roerecke & Rehm 2012 match Tables 2 and 4: 24 fully stratified studies; 44 studies; the 12 fully stratified estimates; occasional 0.82 to 0.98 (Table 2) and 0.87 to 0.97 (Table 4), none significant; all 44 studies 0.62 to 0.81 with every interval excluding 1; I2 up to 84%. 'Lower point estimates at about one drink in all four groups' is correct (0.89, 0.77, 0.84, 0.54). The second-hand former-drinker figures 1.25 (men) and 1.54 (women) are printed here too, as the correction factors taken from Roerecke & Rehm 2011 (ref 36), without intervals. The 'earlier review' is that 2011 paper. The magnitude's description ('against lifetime abstainers; former drinkers excluded and mortality corrected for them') is close, but the statement should name the correction and the uncorrected morbidity strata. Drink labels: the categories are 2.5-11.99, 12-23.99 and 24-35.99 g a day, which the paper labels 1, 2 and 3 standard drinks of 12 g. Strictly they are up to one, one to two, and two to three drinks (recomputed: 11.99/12 = 1.0; 23.99/12 = 2.0; 35.99/12 = 3.0). So 'about one drink' for the lowest category is the paper's label, not its midpoint (about 0.6 drink). Wording otherwise does not overstate. The authors' own conclusion is more cautious than earlier reviews: a cardioprotective association 'cannot be assumed for all drinkers, even at low levels'.

anchors.locator: Abstract › Methods and Results; Methods › Search strategy, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st-3rd paragraphs; Table 1 (Study Design and 'Provided at least one stratified data set' columns)
anchors.extracted: MEDLINE, EMBASE and Web of Science, January 1980 to April 2010, no language restriction. 44 observational studies (Table 1 rows: 32 cohort, 12 case-control) with 38,627 IHD events among 957,684 participants. 24 studies gave fully sex- and end-point-specific estimates (6 of them case-control, all for morbidity); 20 gave only combined estimates. US 16, Japan 5, UK 4. Table 1's title says 43 studies.

anchors.locator: Methods › Data extraction and synthesis, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Former drinkers were excluded from all analyses. Where current non-drinkers were the reference, mortality RRs were corrected on the log scale using the earlier meta-analysis (ref 36, Roerecke & Rehm 2011). Men: former-drinker RR 1.25 times the mean fraction of former drinkers among non-drinkers, 0.32. Women: 1.54 times 0.08. Morbidity RRs were not corrected, because former drinkers' morbidity did not differ significantly from lifetime abstainers'. Intake above 72 g a day was excluded. Estimates had to be at least age-adjusted.

anchors.locator: Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph; Table 2 footnote
anchors.extracted: Categorical analysis against lifetime abstainers: occasional (less than weekly or 0.1-2.49 g a day), 2.5-11.99, 12-23.99, 24-35.99 g a day, described as about 1, 2 and 3 standard drinks of 12 g. Random-effects (DerSimonian-Laird) pooling; Q, I2; Peters test for publication bias.

All 44 studies, including combined sex or end point. Occasional: men's mortality 0.90 (0.76-1.08), men's morbidity 0.87 (0.75-1.01), women's mortality 0.97 (0.84-1.11), women's morbidity 0.92 (0.83-1.02); none significant. At 2.5-11.99 / 12-23.99 / 24-35.99 g a day: men's mortality 0.81, 0.74, 0.74; men's morbidity 0.77, 0.70, 0.66; women's mortality 0.77, 0.74, 0.67; women's morbidity 0.70, 0.69, 0.62. Every upper limit is 0.90 or below.

anchors.locator: Table 3; Results › Continuous dose-response meta-analysis, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Fractional-polynomial curves, stratified studies. Men's mortality: nadir 32 g a day (31 in the text), reversion to harm at 63 g. Men's morbidity: nadir 69 g. Women's mortality: nadir 11 g, reversion 31 g. Women's morbidity: nadir 14 g, reversion 57 g. I2 46-58% (46-59% with all studies). The authors say these curves overstate precision at 1-3 drinks a day compared with the categorical analysis.

Against lifetime abstainers, evidence for a cardioprotective association with IHD mortality was borderline in both sexes at 1-3 drinks a day (upper limits close to or above 1). The authors conclude it cannot be assumed for all drinkers, even at low intake.

Residual confounding cannot be excluded. Adjustment varied widely, and many studies adjusted for age only. Some studies adjusted for prior disease such as angina, stroke or previous myocardial infarction (for example McElduff 1997), so participants with heart disease were not always excluded.

claims.note: The second-hand figure matches: 1.45 (1.24-1.70), from the authors' 2010 meta-analysis (ref 29, Am J Epidemiol 2010). The comparison is drinkers with irregular heavy drinking occasions against drinkers without them, excluding abstainers, former drinkers where possible, occasional drinkers and regular heavy drinkers. So the claim's 'against people who drank without them' names the right reference group. This review also supports the statement that the average-intake review against lifetime abstainers did not take drinking pattern into account: the authors say they could not examine heavy drinking occasions, and suggest these may explain part of the unexplained heterogeneity. The 2010 paper's definition of a heavy occasion and its study count are not given here.

anchors.extracted: Citing their 2010 meta-analysis: drinkers with irregular heavy drinking occasions against drinkers without them, RR 1.45 (95% CI 1.24-1.70). Abstainers, former drinkers where possible, occasional drinkers and regular heavy drinkers were excluded. This review could not investigate such occasions; they may account for much of the unexplained heterogeneity.

anchors.locator: Methods › Search strategy, 1st paragraph (inclusion criterion 4); Methods › Data extraction and synthesis, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Exposure was average consumption only: at least three categories among current drinkers, a reference period over 2 weeks, and usual frequency and volume. No drinking-pattern variable was extracted or analysed.

key_findings.correction: Confirmed: 11 rows have age as the only covariate (Kagan, Colditz, Scragg, Iso, Sempos, Wells, Henderson, Hart, Ikehara 2008 and 2009, Bazzano).
Confirmed. Editors' calculation reproduced: exp(0.32 x ln 1.25) = 1.074; exp(0.08 x ln 1.54) = 1.035.
Confirmed; women's morbidity sample sizes sum to 8,007 (recomputed).
Confirmed: 31 Peters tests (Tables 2 and 4, one NA); one significant (P = 0.01).

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed: P = 0.15 with 10 studies gives Q = 13.29 and I2 = 32.3% (recomputed).
Confirmed: 3 studies, P = 0.63 gives Q = 0.92, I2 0; 4 studies, P = 0.17 gives Q = 5.02, I2 40.3% (recomputed). The values appear transposed.

Narrower than stated. The 'n = 3' sentence comes straight after the women's results in Results › Categorical meta-analysis, 1st paragraph, so it most plausibly refers to the women's strata. It matches women's morbidity (3 studies at 24-35.99 g a day) but not women's mortality (5); it is not a claim about all four strata. The heterogeneity statement (Discussion, 3rd paragraph: all models except women's mortality had substantial unexplained heterogeneity) fits the categorical women's-mortality estimates in Table 2 (P = 0.24, 0.40, 0.10) but not the continuous curve in Table 3 (I2 56%, P = 0.014). Consequence unchanged: use the tables.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2, critically low. Items 2, 7 and 9 fail on any reading. Item 4 'no' follows the project's 25 October convention on unjustified publication-type restrictions (conference abstracts excluded, start in 1980); under a plain AMSTAR reading it could be partial yes, without changing the overall rating. Items 5 and 6 'no' are right: one author did the first screening pass, and extraction is undocumented. Checked: Rehm is an author of refs 49 (Sempos 2002) and 78 (Rehm 1997).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The abstract is cautious and matches the stratified results. The overreach is in Discussion › Implications ('most of the cardioprotective effect can be already achieved' at 1-2 drinks for men and 1 for women; nadirs said to be significant at 33-69 g). The card describes it accurately.

missed: Design mix within the main analyses: 6 of the 24 fully stratified studies are case-control, and all 6 report morbidity (Kaufman 1985, Scragg 1987, Jackson 1991, Romelsjö 2003, Tavani 2004, Dorn 2007; counted from Table 1). So the stratified morbidity estimates rest substantially on case-control data. The card notes this for women only.

The paper does not say how many studies had current non-drinkers as their reference, and so had mortality estimates corrected and morbidity estimates left with former drinkers in the reference group. The 'lifetime abstainer' label in Tables 2 and 4 therefore covers an unknown mix of true lifetime-abstainer comparisons, corrected comparisons and, for morbidity, uncorrected comparisons. Claims should not describe the review as comparing only with lifetime abstainers.

Freedom from heart disease at baseline was not an inclusion criterion: only samples made up entirely of high-risk people were excluded. Some included studies adjusted for prior disease (McElduff 1997: angina, stroke, previous MI; Doll 1994: history of previous disease). Relevant to claims framed as people without heart disease at entry.
